claims.claim: The EN World column's fourth writing step is a halving target for every description, and it names adjectives and adverbs as the writer's enemies.
claims.quote: those words are actually our mortal enemies

claims.claim: The same column argues one well-chosen physical detail can stand for a whole person, instancing the loose skin under an old woman's arm.
claims.quote: it paints a vivid image in your mind of the whole woman

claims.claim: A forum reader rewriting a Bastion of Broken Souls boxed text cuts the phrase 'appears as', calling the hedge a DM reflex the players do not need.
claims.source: forum member 'Dausuul', reply of 15 July 2013 on EN World
claims.quote: "Appears as" is just instinctive DM pedantry

claims.claim: The same reader deletes 'scaly' from the official description on the ground that the noun already carries it.
claims.quote: Scaliness was pure fluff from the start.

claims.claim: Radiating Gnome rewrites an 81-word location description from Dungeon 213 down to 23 words and prints both side by side.
In that rewrite he replaces the causeway's 'rising' with a climbing verb because rising suggests effortless floating.
He keeps an alliteration on purpose, saying the paired sound will stay in the listener's ear.
claims.quote: which will resonate in the listener's ear

claims.claim: He traces the reader's eye through the original passage from feet to cliff to causeway and back, and moves the load-bearing detail forward because listeners are lost after a sentence or two.
claims.quote: That seems like a lot of redirection

claims.claim: Gus L. holds that plain names in a strange world beat strange names in a familiar one, and reads Lost Mine of Phandelver's invented names as unmemorable.
claims.quote: Simple names used in a way that imply a strange world

claims.claim: Gus L. says the Phandalin locations each get a paragraph and no evocative detail in it.
claims.quote: no evocative detail despite having a paragraph each

claims.claim: Gus L. reads a one-line box of read-aloud text in Lost Mine of Phandelver as a symptom of an outdated house style rather than of that scene.
claims.quote: odd devotion to an antiquated house style

claims.claim: Gus L. calls the Phandalin NPC sidebar useless because it gives a name and a note that the person has a quest and nothing else; Bryce Lynch praises the same device.
claims.quote: a simple list of names with "has a quest for party"

claims.claim: Gus L. contrasts the bare category word for a monster with a specific physical description he writes out, arguing the second makes a mystery of the same creature.
claims.quote: is a mystery to be unraveled

claims.claim: David Hartlage's example of boxed text failing is a 2012 tournament room whose load-bearing runes were listed among unimportant details and missed by his whole team.
claims.source: David Hartlage, 'Picturing the dungeon – boxed text', DMDavid
claims.quote: the text mentioned the runes alongside other, less important details

claims.claim: Hartlage attributes boxed text's drag to delivery: a reader's voice takes a different tone and cadence from speech, and the monotony loses the listener.
claims.quote: their voice takes a different tone and cadence
